\chapter{Saying When}
\label{ch:ml-when}
\hlchaptermodality{102}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that something happens on a named day or at a named hour, and ask what time it happens.}

From cold: two answers to \textquotedblleft{}when\textquotedblright{}, and which of the two takes an ending.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ]{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} — at two o'clock}

\label{lesson:ML-C102-manikku}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{two o'clock}. Then say the ending you met as \textbf{to} and \textbf{for} — the one inside \textbf{\ml{എനിക്ക്}}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണി}} \emph{names} an hour. Add the dative and you are no longer naming it — you are putting something \textbf{at} it.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണി}} & \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇi} & two o'clock \\
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}} & \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ} & at two o'clock \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

\textbf{Nothing about the ending is new.} You built this exact landing when you met your first case ending: \textbf{\ml{ജോലി}} ends in the vowel sign \textbf{\ml{ി}}, so it took \textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}} and gave \textbf{\ml{ജോലിക്ക്}}. \textbf{\ml{മണി}} ends in that same vowel and takes that same ending, with the same visible seam — \textbf{\ml{മണി}} plus \textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}}.

\begin{culture}
That first case ending was glossed \textbf{to} and \textbf{for}, and English will not accept either one here: \emph{to two o'clock} is not a thing anybody says. English reaches for a third word, \textbf{at}.

\textbf{That is a fact about English, not about the ending.} Malayalam has not switched cases on you — the suffix on \textbf{\ml{മണിക്ക്}} is letter for letter the one you put on \textbf{\ml{ജോലി}}. What has changed is the English word you need to translate it, and English has three of them where Malayalam has one ending. When you meet this ending on an hour, read it \textbf{at}.
\end{culture}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the slot at the front}]
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും}.} — \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ ñān pōkuṁ} — \textquotedblleft{}At two o'clock I will go.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

You know that slot already. \textbf{\ml{നാളെ}} has stood in it in front of this very sentence. \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} has stood in it too — in front of the same sentence with a \emph{present} ending on the verb, because the day word and the verb ending have to agree. The front is a slot for saying \textbf{when}, and the verb at the back is what carries the tense.

What is new is the toll. \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} walked into that slot wearing nothing. An hour has to put an ending on before it is allowed in.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇi} — naming the hour
  \item \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ} — putting something at it
  \item \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ ñān pōkuṁ}
  \item which chapter you first built this ending on, and on which word
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the difference between \textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണി}} and \textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}}? (\textbf{The first names the hour; the second puts something at it}.) Which ending did you add? (\textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}} — your first case ending.) Why does English need a different word here than it did for \emph{to me}? (\textbf{English splits the job across to, for and at; Malayalam does not}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tiṅkaḷāḻca ñān pōkuṁ]{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും} — on Monday I will go}

\label{lesson:ML-C102-azhcha}



\begin{quote}
Say the day-name for Monday. Then say \emph{at two o'clock}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
The day-name lesson laid all seven of them out in a table and left them there. You have read \textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച}} and never once \emph{used} it. Use it now:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും}.} — \emph{tiṅkaḷāḻca ñān pōkuṁ} — \textquotedblleft{}On Monday I will go.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Read that sentence twice and look for the ending.} There is none. The day-name went into the when-slot exactly as it stands in that table, with nothing added to the front of it and nothing added to the back.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two words, one slot, one ending between them}]
Put the last lesson's sentence beside this one and the difference is the whole point of the chapter:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും}} & \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ…} & the hour took \textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}} \\
\textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും}} & \emph{tiṅkaḷāḻca…} & the day took \textbf{nothing} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both sentences answer \textbf{when}. Both put their answer at the front. One of the two answers had to put an ending on first, and it is the hour.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{The day-name is in good company.} \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} and \textbf{\ml{നാളെ}} stand in that same slot bare, and have since the lesson that first stood a day word in front of a whole sentence. A named day behaves like \emph{today} and \emph{tomorrow}, not like a clock time.

So the line you can rely on, for what this book has taught you, runs between \textbf{the named day} and \textbf{the named hour} — and it is the hour that is the odd one. That is a description of what Malayalam does here, not a law with no exceptions: a day-name can take endings for other jobs. For saying \textbf{when} something happens, it does not need one.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tiṅkaḷāḻca}
  \item \emph{tiṅkaḷāḻca ñān pōkuṁ}
  \item \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ ñān pōkuṁ}, then the Monday line again
  \item which of the two answers carried an ending, and which carried none
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What do you add to \textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച}} to say \emph{on Monday}? (\textbf{Nothing}.) What do you add to \textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണി}} to say \emph{at two}? (\textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}}.) Which two day words stand in that slot bare, the way the day-name does? (\textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} and \textbf{\ml{നാളെ}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[etra maṇikkŭ]{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണിക്ക്} — asking at which hour}

\label{lesson:ML-C102-ethra-manikku}



\begin{quote}
Ask what hour it is — you have been able to since you learned the verb for asking. Then say \emph{at two o'clock}.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണി}} is already yours. The lesson that gave you the verb for \emph{asking} put \emph{etra maṇi} — \textbf{what hour} — in your mouth and drilled it. \textbf{This lesson is one ending away from it.}

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണി}} & \emph{etra maṇi} & what time is it \\
\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണിക്ക്}} & \emph{etra maṇikkŭ} & at what time \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The first asks somebody to \textbf{name} the hour. The second asks \textbf{at which} hour a thing will happen. That is the whole distance between them, and it is the same \textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}} you put on the hour at the start of this chapter.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: which word wears the ending}]
\textbf{\ml{എത്ര}} never changes. Every time you have used it, it has stood in front of a bare noun — \textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{ദൂരം}} (\emph{etra dūraṁ}, how far), \textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{രൂപ}} (\emph{etra rūpa}, how many rupees).

Put a hand over the question word in those two and what is left is a \textbf{distance} and a \textbf{rupee}, standing bare. Do it to \textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണിക്ക്}} and what is left is an hour \textbf{with an ending on it}. The ending is the one thing here the question word did not bring.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
\textbf{The answer comes back wearing the same ending:}

\begin{quote}
— \textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണിക്ക്}?} — \emph{etra maṇikkŭ?} — \textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}.} — \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ.}
\end{quote}

That is worth listening for. A day-name would not do this, because for saying \textbf{when} it does not take the ending in the first place — so there is nothing for it to give back.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{etra maṇi?}, then \emph{etra maṇikkŭ?} — and name the difference
  \item the question, then answer it — \emph{etra maṇikkŭ? raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ.}
  \item \emph{etra dūraṁ}, \emph{etra rūpa}, \emph{etra maṇikkŭ}
  \item which word in the question carries the ending, and which does not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you ask \emph{at what time?} (\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണിക്ക്}}.) What does the same question \emph{without} the ending ask? (\textbf{What time is it} — and you have had that one for a long while.) What does the answer wear? (\textbf{The same ending} — \ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tiṅkaḷāḻca raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ]{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച} \ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} — on Monday at two o'clock}

\label{lesson:ML-C102-day-and-hour}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{on Monday}. Say \emph{at two o'clock}. Now say them one after the other, without stopping.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
You have two answers to \textbf{when}, and real arrangements usually need both:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച} \ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്} \ml{ഞാൻ} \ml{പോകും}.} \emph{tiṅkaḷāḻca raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ ñān pōkuṁ} \textquotedblleft{}On Monday at two o'clock I will go.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\textbf{Neither piece changed to make room for the other.} The day-name is the bare word from the table where you met all seven. The hour is the dative you built at the start of this chapter. They stand side by side in the one slot at the front, and the sentence behind them is untouched.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: wider first}]
The order is not free, and it is the order you would guess: \textbf{the wider container goes first.} A Monday holds a two o'clock; a two o'clock does not hold a Monday.

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
day, then hour & \textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച} \ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}} \\
what English does & \emph{on Monday at two} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

English arranges it the same way, which here is a genuine convenience rather than a trap — you can carry your instinct straight across.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Count what this chapter actually added: \textbf{one ending, on one kind of word.}

Everything else was already yours — the word that names an hour, the table of day-names, the question word you have asked ages and distances and prices with, and the slot at the front that \emph{today} and \emph{tomorrow} stand in. What was missing was never vocabulary. It was the joint, and the joint is \textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}} on the hour and nothing at all on the day.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tiṅkaḷāḻca raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ}
  \item the whole sentence — \emph{…ñān pōkuṁ}
  \item \emph{etra maṇikkŭ?} and answer it with the hour from that sentence
  \item which of the two front words carries an ending, and why the other does not
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which comes first, the day or the hour? (\textbf{The day} — the wider one.) Which of the two carries an ending? (\textbf{The hour}.) What did this chapter add that you did not already own? (\textbf{One ending on one kind of word} — the rest was already yours.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[etra maṇikkŭ enna ōrmma]{(on Monday, at two o'clock, at what time?) — from cold}

\label{lesson:ML-R102-when-recall}



\begin{quote}
Close the lessons before this one. Say \emph{on Monday}, \emph{at two o'clock}, and \emph{at what time?}
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one of them takes an ending}]
Two answers to the same question, and only one of them is dressed:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച}} & \emph{tiṅkaḷāḻca} & on Monday — \textbf{bare} \\
\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}} & \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ} & at two o'clock — \textbf{\ml{ക്ക്}} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

If you can remember which one is which, you have the chapter. The day-name stands in the when-slot the way \textbf{\ml{ഇന്ന്}} and \textbf{\ml{നാളെ}} have stood there since a day word first went in front of a whole sentence. The hour does not; it takes the dative first.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
\textbf{No word in this chapter was new.} That is unusual enough to say out loud. The hour came from the lesson that named it, the day-names from their table, the question word from the day you asked somebody their age, and the ending itself from your first case ending — where it meant \emph{to} and \emph{for} and landed on \textbf{\ml{ജോലി}} exactly as it now lands on \textbf{\ml{മണി}}.

What you could not do before was \textbf{fix an arrangement in time} — and what was missing was one joint, not a vocabulary list.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{tiṅkaḷāḻca}, then \emph{raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ}
  \item \emph{etra maṇikkŭ?} and answer it
  \item \emph{tiṅkaḷāḻca raṇṭŭ maṇikkŭ ñān pōkuṁ}
  \item the two day words that behave like the day-name
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
\emph{On Monday}? (\textbf{\ml{തിങ്കളാഴ്ച}} — nothing added.) \emph{At two o'clock}? (\textbf{\ml{രണ്ട്} \ml{മണിക്ക്}}.) \emph{At what time?} (\textbf{\ml{എത്ര} \ml{മണിക്ക്}}.) Which comes first when you say both? (\textbf{The day}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
